items.title: Even stupendous black holes can’t explain dark matter
items.summary: The theoretical objects would have left a larger imprint on cosmic radiation if they were a source of the invisible force pulling together the galaxies.

items.title: Could a giant sunshade in space ‘solve global warming’? Scientists are taking the idea seriously
items.summary: Some say the concept is complete fantasy, but a detailed analysis suggests that the falling cost of rocket launches might make it feasible in a few decades.

items.title: Record-breaking retraction: scholarly publisher pulls 1,400 conference papers on one day
items.summary: Announcement by IEEE follows publication of a study showing the retracted papers are linked to paper mills.

items.title: The brain liquidates billions of mutant neurons around the time we’re born
items.summary: Faulty neurons can contribute to various neurological conditions, but researchers have uncovered a system that might clean them up.

items.title: Genetic variants that alter gene regulation in specific cell types are closely tied to disease
items.summary: Single-cell profiling of nearly 2,000 people brings scientists closer to understanding the link between genetic variation, gene expression and health.

items.title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking
items.summary: Computational simulations of a neural network based on fly connectomes identify a three-neuron circuit that is organized to produce leg motor rhythms for walking.

items.title: Clues about complex life come from freshly cultivated archaea
items.summary: Two archaeal strains that belong to a lineage closely related to the ancestor of eukaryotic cells (complex cells with membrane-bound organelles) have been brought into culture. Their simple internal organization, elaborate surface structures, microbial partnerships and protein-dependent lifestyle provide clues about how eukaryotic cells arose.

items.title: Ribbon made of carbon pentagons and heptagons has metallic properties
items.summary: Ribbons that are composed exclusively of five- and seven-carbon rings have metal-like electron transport and conductance. The ribbons can be synthesized by linking previously inaccessible chains of paired five-membered rings, providing a route to making highly conducting carbon nanoribbons.

items.title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury
items.summary: A subset of necrotizing enterocolitis in infants is mediated specifically by the Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin.

items.title: Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression
items.summary: Whole-genome sequencing and cell-level gene expression measurements show that length variation in tandem repeats in the human genome contributes to cell type-specific differences in gene regulation and expression, as well as the architecture of complex traits.

items.title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons
items.summary: Single-neuron sequencing shows that widespread genomic abnormalities are common prenatally but largely eliminated around birth, indicating developmental genome quality control in human neurons.

items.title: Measles made a stealthy return as another virus took the spotlight
items.summary: Vaccination rates dropped after the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted public-health programmes and their funding.

items.title: Iranian scientists in the United States face major upheaval
items.summary: Pressures due to the continuing US–Iran conflict are mounting as early-career researchers endure frozen immigration status, employment limbo and families caught in the war.

items.title: Five overlooked steps to identify new epidemics, fast
items.summary: Current measures to track emerging epidemics have a key limitation: they don’t work if the disease causes unusual or unexpected symptoms.

items.title: How researchers debunked ‘race science’: ‘a triumph of scientific self-correction’
items.summary: An account of how nineteenth-century studies aiming to find a biological basis for human races were dismantled by good scientific practices — although their effects are still felt today.

items.title: How the US mid-term elections could shake up science
items.summary: A Democratic victory in Congress could halt the Trump administration’s controversial grant-review plan and curb some of its funding actions.

items.title: Lactate takes a shortcut into mitochondria to power the heart
items.summary: A cellular fuel called lactate is channelled directly into energy-generating organelles in heart muscle, defying the prevailing view about lactate transport.

items.title: Dengue comes back even in vaccinated people — new clues
items.summary: Researchers help to answer a question dogging the development of improved vaccines against the mosquito-borne disease.

items.title: How the pandemic changed trust in science — in four charts
items.summary: The largest analysis of its kind reveals the public’s changing relationship with science and the people who do it.

items.title: Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor
items.summary: Pseudo-direct bandgap character in bismuth sulfide retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination while preserving strong light absorption.

items.title: Narrow carbon pentaheptite nanoribbon as a covalent metal
items.summary: Planar carbon pentaheptite nanoribbons are synthesized by laterally fusing polypentalene chains transformed from pre-synthesized polycyclooctadiene chains, suggesting a possible route towards carbon quantum wires.

items.title: Earth’s resources sustain humanity — but they come at a high price
items.summary: Two books explore the damage caused by our unsustainable extraction of raw materials.

items.title: I built the UK government’s metascience unit — here’s what countries need to know
items.summary: To find evidence-backed ways to improve grant-funding processes, metascientists need freedom and money to experiment, as well as leaders who are willing to make change.

items.title: Are dinosaur fossils hogging top journals? Analysis sparks debate over ‘charismatic’ finds
items.summary: Fossils of dinosaurs, mammals and other glamorous species are over-represented in high-profile titles, suggests a study of thousands of palaeontology papers.

items.title: Daily briefing: The three red flags of suspicious journals
items.summary: These warning signs suggest a journal might be engaging in dubious publishing activities. Plus, the brain clears out faulty neurons at birth and whether a giant ‘sunshade’ could cool Earth.

items.title: Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination
items.summary: Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination

items.title: Accounting of Africa’s water reveals a management gap
items.summary: A map of Africa’s water demand reveals that the scarcity of water is only part of the problem facing the continent — management is a separate challenge.

items.title: Daily briefing: The big push to personalize psychiatry
items.summary: A data-driven approach could match treatments to individuals with more precision. Plus, funders in Europe are backing preprint-led publishing and whether professors should care about student evaluations.

items.title: How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry
items.summary: Fresh ideas are welcome in a discipline in which progress is rare — provided they are applied rigorously.

items.title: Meta-study sparks questions about what it means to be good at regulating emotions
items.summary: A first-of-its kind consortium reveals a lack of correlation between behavioural and neural measures of a person’s emotional regulation.

items.title: Molecular underpinnings of rheumatic diseases and emerging therapeutic concepts
items.summary: Improved molecular insights into inflammatory rheumatic diseases are enabling better disease control and advancing the field towards achieving durable remission and eventual cure.

items.title: In Indonesia, PhD students blow the whistle on bad supervision
items.summary: The nation plans to boost the number of doctoral candidates, but some early-career researchers warn of systemic challenges, including poor-quality supervision.

items.title: Briefing Chat: Dog years: could longevity science extend your pets' lives?
items.summary: Nature staff discuss the emerging field of pet longevity — plus, a researcher decides not to care about their student reviews. Are they wrong?

items.title: Why did ancient humans avoid this lush paradise
items.summary: A new expedition into the Rub’ al Khali desert finds no evidence of ancient human settlement.

items.title: This Arabian desert was once a lush paradise. Why did ancient humans avoid it?
items.summary: Expedition revealed that water wasn’t enough for human settlement — plus, proposals to block sunlight get serious.

items.title: Tethered to stone: how rock and water availability shaped early desert occupation
items.summary: Fresh water in deserts often points to sites with signs of early humans and stone tools. But, in Arabia’s Rub’ al Khali region, water alone does not predict occupation.

items.title: Preprint-centric publishing model gets major boost
items.summary: European funders put weight behind emerging ‘publish, review, curate’ approach for preprints.

items.title: These three red flags could unmask dodgy journals
items.summary: As poor publishing practices proliferate, scholarly databases are under pressure to ensure the titles they list are reputable.

items.title: Is research funding now a lottery? Elite funder ERC swamped by applications
items.summary: A marked rise in submissions for the European Research Council’s grants is pushing down success rates.

items.title: The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care
items.summary: Could a blood sample, a brain scan and a look at your phone data transform how your psychiatrist treats you?

items.title: An unexpected function of a cell-cycle enzyme might explain the toxic effects of its inhibitors
items.summary: A previously unknown mechanism required for cells to start proliferating has been identified. A combination of mathematical modelling and cell-based experiments shows that the enzyme WEE1 switches off a protein-degradation complex to allow cell proliferation to start, with implications for WEE1 inhibitors currently in trials for cancer treatments.

items.title: Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
items.summary: A geoarchaeological survey of the Rub’ al Khali (the Empty Quarter of Arabia) and spatial modelling of the Arabian Peninsula suggest that human settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and stone suitable for making tools, rather than water alone.

items.title: Patrick Stewart dies: how Captain Picard inspired today’s science leaders
items.summary: Researchers say his portrayal of the Star Trek character represented curiosity, thoughtfulness and an effort to understand others.

items.title: Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions
items.summary: Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions

items.title: What students think about my teaching doesn’t matter. Am I wrong?
items.summary: A jury weighs in on whether teaching assessments are popularity contests or an important tool.

items.title: The shifting sands of research independence: why mid-career scientists crave security
items.summary: A project to improve understanding of an often-neglected group in academia aims to help its members to navigate career uncertainty.

items.title: Author Correction: mTORC1 drives cell-autonomous astrocyte reactivity in tuberous sclerosis
items.summary: Author Correction: mTORC1 drives cell-autonomous astrocyte reactivity in tuberous sclerosis

items.title: Author Correction: Rh<sup>3+</sup> stabilized in KRh@MFI catalyses regioselective hydroformylation
items.summary: Author Correction: Rh 3+ stabilized in KRh@MFI catalyses regioselective hydroformylation
